audience.programmeDescription: VU Earth Sciences, Economics and Sustainability connects physical Earth systems with economic choices and spatial sustainability problems. Students study climate risk, water, land, energy and resources using field research, data analysis and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers an integrated Earth, water, risk and biodiversity programme, a resource and energy programme with greater economic evaluation, and a computational direction combining environmental science with programming and machine learning. Spatial analysis, laboratory and field activities support these related responses. Dedicated environmental economics, advanced sustainability-specific data science, environmental ethics, VU’s specified fieldwork and the individual thesis remain important differences. Computational courses provide general methods; particular environmental project topics are not guaranteed.

curriculum.routeLabel: Ordinary full-time bachelor; Urban Challenges restricted elective
curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC comprises 144 EC of required courses, one 6 EC restricted choice and 30 EC of free study. Fieldwork preparation requires 24 eligible first-year EC; second-year fieldwork requires 60 EC including the first fieldwork. Thesis entry requires 126 EC including recognised fieldwork. Free-choice courses have level and approval rules. The first-year study-advice norm is 42 EC. A language test or remediation gates the Soil and Landscape grade; mentoring and Geoflex obligations carry no credits.

concepts.label: Earth systems, economics and sustainable development
concepts.concept: Combine Earth and climate science, soils, water and biodiversity with economics, quantitative methods and sustainability governance. Geological and laboratory fieldwork, GIS and spatial projects connect physical evidence with adaptation and energy decisions; dedicated environmental economics, advanced sustainability data science and the individual VU thesis remain important gaps.

concepts.label: Resources, energy and economic evaluation
concepts.concept: Connect Earth-resource science with energy-system analysis, renewable design, resource recovery and life-cycle assessment. Five economics courses add 37.5 EC of theory, public-policy analysis and econometrics, giving this direction greater economic and technical energy weight than the integrated water, risk and biodiversity programme.

concepts.label: Environmental modelling, spatial data and machine learning
concepts.concept: Combine Earth systems, water and delta systems, geospatial analysis and physical environmental investigation with programming, algorithms, machine learning and neural prediction. The computational courses supply general methods for environmental questions supported by the science courses; particular environmental project topics are not guaranteed, and specialist environmental economics, ethics and the VU thesis remain gaps.

notes.text: These UCR programmes combine substantial Earth and sustainability study with different economic or computational priorities. They do not reproduce dedicated environmental economics, physical hydrology and nature-management depth, environmental ethics, VU’s two specified fieldwork units or its required individual 12-EC thesis. Data and machine-learning courses supply general methods alongside environmental science, rather than the same sustainability Big Data course. Optional independent research requires approval and is outside the 24-course schedules; it does not replace the VU thesis.

selectedModalDescriptions.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

selectedModalDescriptions.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

selectedModalDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
